objectives: Students will identify forms of energy and trace energy conversions using the law of conservation of energy.
Students will calculate kinetic energy (KE = ½mv<sup>2</sup>) and gravitational potential energy (PE = mgh).
Students will distinguish conduction, convection, and radiation and interpret heat-transfer data.

teach:
Week 9 Science: Energy and Waves — Forms of Energy, Conservation, Heat Transfer, Waves, and Electricity

Objectives

  • Name the main forms of energy and trace energy conversions in everyday devices and events.
  • Apply the law of conservation of energy, including energy “lost” to thermal energy through friction.
  • Calculate kinetic energy (KE = ½mv2) and gravitational potential energy (PE = mgh).
  • Identify conduction, convection, and radiation, and describe waves using wavelength, frequency, amplitude, and speed (v = f × λ), including the order of the electromagnetic spectrum.
  • Use Ohm’s law (V = IR) to solve simple circuit problems and read data tables and graphs about energy and electricity.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors.
  • Calculators (students may use one on the GED Science test).
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week’s Student Lesson and Study Notes.
  • Optional demo items: a metal spoon and a plastic spoon, a cup of hot water, a rope or slinky for making waves.
  • This week’s 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Where does the energy go?” Trace four everyday energy conversions.
Direct instruction20Forms of energy, conservation, KE and PE formulas, heat transfer, waves and the electromagnetic spectrum, circuits and Ohm’s law; Worked Examples 1–5.
Guided practice15Five short calculation and identification problems, solved together.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (finish for homework if needed).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; preview the exit ticket and this week’s Practice GED.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write these four situations on the board. Ask: “What form of energy goes in, and what form or forms come out?”

  1. A toaster browns a slice of bread.
  2. A person eats lunch and then rides a bicycle up a hill.
  3. A solar panel on a roof powers a ceiling fan.
  4. A firework explodes in the night sky.

Answers: (1) Electrical → thermal (and some light from the glowing coils). (2) Chemical energy in food → kinetic energy of the moving rider and bicycle → gravitational potential energy as the rider climbs; some becomes thermal energy (the rider gets warm). (3) Light (radiant) energy → electrical → kinetic energy of the spinning blades (plus a little sound and thermal energy). (4) Chemical → light, sound, thermal, and kinetic energy of the flying pieces.

Point to make: In every case, energy changed form, but none appeared from nothing and none disappeared. That is the big idea of today’s lesson.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. What energy is. Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. It is measured in joules (J). Energy comes in two big families:

  • Kinetic energy — energy of motion. Anything moving has it: a rolling ball, flowing water, vibrating air (sound), moving electric charges (electrical energy), jiggling particles (thermal energy).
  • Potential energy — stored energy due to position or arrangement: a book on a high shelf (gravitational), a stretched rubber band (elastic), food, fuel, and batteries (chemical), the center of an atom (nuclear).

Light, or radiant energy, is energy carried by electromagnetic waves; treat it as its own form.

2. The law of conservation of energy. Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it only changes form or moves from one object to another. The total amount stays the same. When a GED question says energy was “lost,” it almost always means energy turned into thermal energy (heat) through friction or air resistance and spread into the surroundings. It did not vanish.

Energy in = energy out. Useful energy out + “wasted” energy (usually thermal) = total energy in.

3. Kinetic and potential energy formulas. Write both on the board and keep them up all lesson.

KE = ½mv2   m = mass in kilograms (kg), v = speed in meters per second (m/s), KE in joules (J)

PE = mgh   m = mass (kg), g = 9.8 m/s2 (gravity on Earth), h = height in meters (m), PE in joules (J)

Stress the order of operations in KE: square the speed first, then multiply by the mass, then take half. Because speed is squared, doubling speed makes KE four times as large. In PE, all three numbers are simply multiplied, so doubling height doubles PE.

Worked Example 1 (kinetic energy). A 1,200 kg car travels at 15 m/s. What is its kinetic energy? What would it be at 30 m/s?

KE = ½ × 1,200 × 152
152 = 225
½ × 1,200 = 600
600 × 225 = 135,000 J

At 30 m/s: 302 = 900; 600 × 900 = 540,000 J. The speed doubled, and the KE became 540,000 ÷ 135,000 = 4 times as large. This is why highway crashes are so much more damaging than low-speed crashes.

Worked Example 2 (potential energy). A 60 kg hiker climbs to a lookout 150 m above the trailhead. How much gravitational potential energy has she gained?

PE = mgh = 60 × 9.8 × 150
60 × 9.8 = 588
588 × 150 = 88,200 J

Worked Example 3 (conservation of energy). A 500 kg roller coaster car starts at rest at the top of a 30 m hill. (a) What is its PE at the top? (b) With no friction, what would its KE be at the bottom? (c) Sensors show its actual KE at the bottom is 132,300 J. Where did the rest of the energy go?

(a) PE = 500 × 9.8 × 30 = 4,900 × 30 = 147,000 J. At rest, KE = 0, so total energy = 147,000 J.
(b) All of the PE becomes KE: 147,000 J.
(c) 147,000 − 132,300 = 14,700 J was converted to thermal energy (and some sound) by friction with the track and air resistance. That is 14,700 ÷ 147,000 = 0.10 = 10% of the starting energy. The energy was not destroyed; it changed into forms that are not useful for moving the car.

4. Heat transfer. Thermal energy always moves from a warmer object to a cooler one, never the other way on its own. “Cold” does not flow into things; heat flows out of them. There are three ways it moves:

MethodHow it worksExample
ConductionDirect contact; fast particles bump slower ones. Best in solids, especially metals.A pan handle heats up on the stove.
ConvectionWarm fluid (liquid or gas) rises, cooler fluid sinks, forming a current that carries heat.A space heater warms a whole room; boiling water churns.
RadiationElectromagnetic waves (mostly infrared) carry energy; needs no matter, so it works through empty space.The Sun warms Earth; you feel a campfire’s heat from a distance.

Quick demo: put a metal spoon and a plastic spoon in hot water. After a minute, the metal handle is warm and the plastic is not. Metal is a good conductor; plastic is an insulator. Insulators such as foam, wool, and fiberglass slow heat transfer, often by trapping air.

5. Waves. A wave is a disturbance that carries energy from place to place without carrying matter along with it. Shake a rope (or slinky) to show it.

  • Wavelength (λ): distance from one crest to the next crest, in meters.
  • Frequency (f): number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz). 1 Hz = 1 wave per second.
  • Amplitude: height of a crest from the resting position. Bigger amplitude = more energy (louder sound, brighter light, taller ocean wave).
  • Speed: v = f × λ, in meters per second.

Mechanical waves (sound, water waves, earthquake waves) need a medium; sound cannot travel through empty space. Electromagnetic waves (light, radio, X-rays) can travel through a vacuum, and all of them move at the speed of light, 3.0 × 108 m/s. Point out that for waves at the same speed, higher frequency means shorter wavelength.

Worked Example 4 (wave speed). (a) Water waves in a lake have a frequency of 2.0 Hz and a wavelength of 3.0 m. What is their speed? (b) An FM radio station broadcasts at 1.0 × 108 Hz. Radio waves travel at 3.0 × 108 m/s. What is the wavelength?

(a) v = f × λ = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 m/s.
(b) Rearrange: λ = v ÷ f = (3.0 × 108) ÷ (1.0 × 108) = 3.0 m.

6. The electromagnetic spectrum. Give students the order and a memory sentence: Rabbits Meet In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens.

Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet) → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma ray

Left to right: wavelength gets shorter, frequency gets higher, and energy per wave gets higher. That is why ultraviolet causes sunburn and X-rays and gamma rays can damage cells, while radio waves are harmless.

7. Electricity and simple circuits. A circuit is a closed loop that lets charges flow. It needs a source (battery or outlet), wires (conductors), and a load (bulb, motor). An open switch breaks the loop and current stops.

  • Voltage (V), in volts: the “push” that moves charges.
  • Current (I), in amperes or amps (A): how much charge flows per second.
  • Resistance (R), in ohms (Ω): how much the material opposes the flow.

Ohm’s law: V = I × R. Rearranged: I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. Cover the one you want in the triangle (V on top, I and R on the bottom).

Series circuit: one path; resistances add (Rtotal = R1 + R2); if one bulb burns out, all go out. Parallel circuit: several paths; if one bulb burns out, the others stay lit (this is how homes are wired).

Worked Example 5 (Ohm’s law). (a) A 9.0 V battery is connected to a 3.0 Ω resistor. What is the current? (b) A lamp plugged into a 120 V outlet draws 0.50 A. What is its resistance? (c) A 12 V battery runs a series circuit with a 4.0 Ω and a 2.0 Ω resistor. What is the current?

(a) I = V ÷ R = 9.0 ÷ 3.0 = 3.0 A.
(b) R = V ÷ I = 120 ÷ 0.50 = 240 Ω.
(c) Rtotal = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 Ω; I = 12 ÷ 6.0 = 2.0 A.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work these one at a time. Have students write the formula first, then substitute, then calculate with units. Call on different students for each step.

  1. A 7.0 kg bowling ball rolls at 4.0 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
  2. A 2.0 kg textbook sits on a shelf 1.5 m above the floor. Find its gravitational potential energy.
  3. A wave on a rope has a frequency of 5.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.40 m. Find its speed.
  4. A phone charger supplies 5.0 V and pushes 2.0 A of current through a device. Find the device’s resistance.
  5. Name the method of heat transfer: (a) hot air from a hair dryer warms a cold room; (b) your hand warms an ice cube you are holding; (c) a heat lamp keeps food warm from above.

Answers:
1. KE = ½ × 7.0 × 4.02 = ½ × 7.0 × 16 = 3.5 × 16 = 56 J.
2. PE = 2.0 × 9.8 × 1.5 = 19.6 × 1.5 = 29.4 J.
3. v = 5.0 × 0.40 = 2.0 m/s.
4. R = V ÷ I = 5.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.5 Ω.
5. (a) Convection (moving warm air carries the heat). (b) Conduction (direct contact; heat flows from the warmer hand into the cooler ice). (c) Radiation (infrared waves travel from the lamp to the food).

Checks for Understanding

  1. “A ball’s speed triples. What happens to its kinetic energy?” Expected: it becomes 32 = 9 times as large.
  2. “Which method of heat transfer can move energy through empty space, and why?” Expected: radiation, because electromagnetic waves do not need matter to travel.
  3. “Two waves travel at the same speed. Wave A has twice the frequency of wave B. Compare their wavelengths.” Expected: wave A has half the wavelength of wave B.
  4. “If the voltage stays the same and the resistance goes up, what happens to the current?” Expected: the current goes down (I = V ÷ R).
  5. “A machine takes in 500 J and does 400 J of useful work. Where did the other 100 J go?” Expected: it changed into thermal energy (and possibly sound); it was not destroyed.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Squaring at the wrong time (or not at all). Students compute ½ × 60 × 5 = 150 instead of ½ × 60 × 25 = 750. Fix: always write “v2 = ___” as its own line before anything else.

Forgetting the ½ in KE. 60 × 25 = 1,500 is a common wrong choice on the test. Fix: say the formula aloud as “half m v squared” and check whether your answer is half of mass × speed2.

Saying energy was “used up” or “destroyed.” Fix: ask, “What form did it change into?” The answer is almost always thermal energy from friction or air resistance.

Thinking cold flows. “The ice pack sends cold into my knee.” Fix: heat leaves the warmer knee and flows into the cooler ice pack.

Mixing up frequency and wavelength in v = f × λ. Students divide when they should multiply. Fix: check units. Hz is “per second,” so (1/s) × m = m/s, a speed.

Reversing the electromagnetic spectrum. Students think radio waves have the most energy because radio signals travel far. Fix: use the memory sentence and the rule “shorter wavelength = higher frequency = more energy.”

Differentiation

Support: Give students a formula card with each formula, each variable’s name, and its unit. Use whole numbers first (m = 2, v = 3) before decimals. For Ohm’s law, draw the V-over-I-R triangle and let students cover the unknown with a finger. For heat transfer, use the hand signals: touching palms (conduction), a hand rising in a circle (convection), fingers spreading outward (radiation).

Stretch: (1) Use conservation of energy to find speed: a 2.0 kg ball dropped from 5.0 m has PE = 2.0 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 98 J; at the bottom, 98 = ½ × 2.0 × v2, so v2 = 98 and v ≈ 9.9 m/s. Notice the mass cancels: any object dropped from 5.0 m (ignoring air resistance) lands at about 9.9 m/s. (2) Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%. A bulb that turns 60 J of electrical energy into 6 J of light is 10% efficient. (3) Electric power: P = V × I, in watts. A 120 V lamp drawing 0.50 A uses 60 W.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Calculation items give you the formula in the question or the passage, such as “Kinetic energy can be calculated with KE = ½mv2.” Your job is to substitute correctly and use your calculator. Answer choices usually include the results of common mistakes (no ½, no squaring).
  • Fill-in-the-blank items ask for a number, such as “What is the current, in amperes, through the resistor?”
  • Data items show a table or graph (temperature over time for different insulators; current for different resistors; speed at different heights) and ask you to find a value, describe a trend, or pick the conclusion the data support.
  • Energy-conversion items describe a device or event and ask which sequence of energy forms is correct.
  • Drag-and-drop and drop-down items ask you to sort examples into conduction, convection, and radiation, or complete statements about waves and circuits.
  • Typical wording: “Which statement best explains why…”, “Based on the data, what would most likely…”, “According to the law of conservation of energy…”

Remind students that this week’s Practice GED covers the whole science test, so energy and waves will appear alongside life science and earth science items.
student:
Energy and Waves: How Energy Moves and Changes

Energy is behind everything that happens: a car moving, a phone charging, the Sun warming your skin. On the GED Science test, you will trace how energy changes form, use a few simple formulas, and read data about heat, waves, and electricity. When a question needs a formula, it is usually given in the question or the passage, so focus on knowing what each letter means and how to plug in numbers.

1. Forms of energy

Energy is the ability to do work or cause change. It is measured in joules (J).

  • Kinetic energy is energy of motion: a rolling ball, wind, sound, electric current, and thermal energy (moving particles).
  • Potential energy is stored energy: a rock at the top of a cliff (gravitational), a stretched spring (elastic), food, gasoline, and batteries (chemical), and the center of atoms (nuclear).
  • Light (radiant energy) is energy carried by electromagnetic waves.

Energy often changes form. A flashlight turns chemical energy (battery) into electrical energy, then into light and some thermal energy.

2. Energy is conserved

Law of conservation of energy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed. It only changes form or moves to another object. The total stays the same.

When a test question says energy was “lost,” ask yourself what it turned into. Usually, friction or air resistance changed some of it into thermal energy, which spread into the surroundings.

3. Calculating kinetic and potential energy

KE = ½mv2 (m = mass in kg, v = speed in m/s)
PE = mgh (m = mass in kg, g = 9.8 m/s2, h = height in m)

Steps for KE: (1) square the speed; (2) multiply by the mass; (3) divide by 2. For PE, just multiply the three numbers.

Example 1. A 50 kg skateboarder rolls at 4.0 m/s. Find her kinetic energy.

v2 = 4.0 × 4.0 = 16
50 × 16 = 800
800 ÷ 2 = 400 J

Example 2. A 3.0 kg flower pot sits on a balcony 8.0 m above the ground. Find its gravitational potential energy.

PE = 3.0 × 9.8 × 8.0
3.0 × 9.8 = 29.4
29.4 × 8.0 = 235.2 J

If the pot fell, this PE would turn into KE. Just before it hit the ground (ignoring air resistance), it would have about 235 J of kinetic energy.

Watch the square. Because speed is squared, doubling speed makes KE four times as large. Doubling mass or height only doubles the energy.

4. Heat transfer

Thermal energy (heat) always flows from warmer to cooler. It moves in three ways:

MethodHowExample
ConductionDirect touchA metal spoon in hot soup gets hot.
ConvectionWarm liquid or gas rises and circulatesWarm air from a heater spreads around a room.
RadiationElectromagnetic waves; works through empty spaceSunlight warms your face.

Conductors (such as metals) let heat move easily. Insulators (such as foam, wool, and plastic) slow it down.

5. Waves

A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying matter with it.

  • Wavelength (λ): distance from one crest to the next, in meters.
  • Frequency (f): number of waves per second, in hertz (Hz).
  • Amplitude: the height of the wave. Larger amplitude means more energy (a louder sound or a brighter light).

Wave speed: v = f × λ

Example 3. A sound wave has a frequency of 170 Hz and a wavelength of 2.0 m. What is its speed?

v = 170 × 2.0 = 340 m/s

Sound, water waves, and earthquake waves need matter to travel through. Electromagnetic waves do not; they all travel through space at 3.0 × 108 m/s. Here is the electromagnetic spectrum from longest wavelength to shortest:

Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma ray

Moving to the right, frequency and energy increase. Memory sentence: Rabbits Meet In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens.

6. Electricity and Ohm’s law

A circuit is a closed path for electric current. It needs a power source, wires, and something that uses the energy, such as a bulb.

  • Voltage (V), in volts: the push.
  • Current (I), in amperes (A): the flow.
  • Resistance (R), in ohms (Ω): what slows the flow.

Ohm’s law: V = I × R   so   I = V ÷ R   and   R = V ÷ I

Example 4. A 6.0 V battery is connected to a bulb with a resistance of 12 Ω. What is the current?

I = V ÷ R = 6.0 ÷ 12 = 0.50 A

In a series circuit there is one path, so if one bulb goes out, they all go out. In a parallel circuit there are several paths, so the other bulbs stay lit.

Common mistake: If voltage stays the same and resistance goes up, current goes down. They move in opposite directions.

Try It

1. A 0.15 kg baseball is thrown at 40 m/s. What is its kinetic energy? (KE = ½mv2)

Show answer

v2 = 40 × 40 = 1,600. Then 0.15 × 1,600 = 240. Then 240 ÷ 2 = 120 J.

2. A 5.0 kg box sits on a shelf 2.0 m high. What is its gravitational potential energy? (PE = mgh, g = 9.8 m/s2)

Show answer

PE = 5.0 × 9.8 × 2.0 = 49 × 2.0 = 98 J.

3. An ocean wave has a frequency of 0.20 Hz and a wavelength of 25 m. What is its speed?

Show answer

v = f × λ = 0.20 × 25 = 5.0 m/s.

4. A current of 0.25 A flows through a 48 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it?

Show answer

V = I × R = 0.25 × 48 = 12 V.

5. You hold an ice cube and it starts to melt. Which way does heat flow, and by which method?

Show answer

Heat flows from your warmer hand into the cooler ice cube by conduction (direct contact).
post:
Post Lesson: Energy and Waves

Summary of Key Points

  • Energy is the ability to cause change, measured in joules. Kinetic energy is energy of motion; potential energy is stored energy.
  • Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed in form. “Lost” energy usually became thermal energy through friction.
  • KE = ½mv2 (square the speed first). PE = mgh with g = 9.8 m/s2.
  • Heat flows from warmer to cooler by conduction (touch), convection (moving fluid), or radiation (electromagnetic waves, even through space).
  • Waves carry energy. v = f × λ. Larger amplitude means more energy.
  • Electromagnetic spectrum, long to short wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy.
  • Ohm’s law: V = IR. At the same voltage, more resistance means less current.

Exit Ticket

1. A 4.0 kg cart moves at 3.0 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

Show answer

v2 = 9.0; 4.0 × 9.0 = 36; 36 ÷ 2 = 18 J.

2. How does energy from the Sun reach Earth, and why can’t it be conduction or convection?

Show answer

Radiation. Space is nearly empty, and conduction and convection both need matter. Electromagnetic waves can travel through empty space.

3. A wave has a frequency of 10 Hz and a wavelength of 0.50 m. What is its speed?

Show answer

v = 10 × 0.50 = 5.0 m/s.

4. A 6.0 V battery is connected to a 2.0 Ω resistor. What is the current?

Show answer

I = V ÷ R = 6.0 ÷ 2.0 = 3.0 A.

5. A truck doubles its speed. By what factor does its kinetic energy change?

Show answer

Speed is squared, so 22 = 4 times as much kinetic energy.

Reflection

  1. Pick one device you used today (a phone, a stove, a car). Trace its energy conversions from start to finish. Where does some energy end up as thermal energy?
  2. Which formula this week felt most comfortable, and which one do you need to practice more? What step tends to trip you up?
  3. Think about your home in winter or summer. Where does heat get in or out, and is it by conduction, convection, or radiation?

This Week’s Study Plan

DayTask (20–40 minutes)
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Make a formula card with KE, PE, v = f × λ, and V = IR, including units.
Day 2Do the 12 practice items. For every miss, read the explanation and redo the problem on paper.
Day 3Heat transfer and waves: write two home examples each of conduction, convection, and radiation. Say the electromagnetic spectrum memory sentence until you can write it from memory.
Day 4Calculation drill: make up three KE, three PE, and three Ohm’s law problems with friendly numbers and solve them. Check by working backward.
Day 5Take this week’s Practice GED (90 minutes, timed). Use the full time.
Day 6Review every Practice GED item you missed. Sort your misses by topic (life, physical, earth and space) and note your weakest area.
Day 7Rest, or review the Study Notes for 20 minutes. Next week covers earth and space science and a full review.

Test-Taking Strategy: Write the Formula, Then Substitute

On a calculation item, do not punch numbers straight into the calculator. First write the formula on your scratch paper. Next, write each number under its letter with its unit. Then calculate one step at a time. Finally, check whether your answer matches a choice made from a common mistake, such as forgetting the ½ or forgetting to square. If your answer is exactly double or exactly the square root of another choice, slow down and check that step.

notes:
Study Notes: Energy and Waves

Formulas (units)

  • KE = ½mv2 — J; m in kg; v in m/s
  • PE = mgh — J; g = 9.8 m/s2; h in m
  • v = f × λ — m/s; f in Hz; λ in m
  • V = I × R — volts; amps (A); ohms (Ω)
    I = V ÷ R   R = V ÷ I
  • Series: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + …

Key Rules

  • Energy is never created or destroyed; it changes form.
  • “Lost” energy = thermal energy from friction.
  • Double speed → 4 × KE. Double height → 2 × PE.
  • Heat flows warm → cool, never the reverse on its own.
  • Same voltage, more resistance → less current.
  • Bigger amplitude → more energy (louder, brighter).

Forms of Energy

Kinetic: motion, thermal, sound, electrical
Potential: gravitational, elastic, chemical, nuclear
Light: carried by electromagnetic waves

Electromagnetic Spectrum

Radio → Microwave → Infrared → Visible → Ultraviolet → X-ray → Gamma
Longer λ, lower f, less energy  →  shorter λ, higher f, more energy
Rabbits Meet In Very Unusual eXpensive Gardens

Waves

Mechanical (sound, water) need matter. Electromagnetic waves travel through space at 3.0 × 108 m/s.

Heat transferHowExample
ConductionDirect contact (best in metals)Hot pan handle
ConvectionWarm fluid rises, cool fluid sinksHeater warms a room
RadiationElectromagnetic waves; no matter neededSun warms Earth

stimuli.title: Pendulum Energy Investigation
stimuli.html:
A physics class studied energy in a pendulum. They hung a 0.50 kg metal ball from a long string. For each trial, they pulled the ball to the side until it was a measured height above its lowest point, held it still, and released it. A motion sensor recorded the ball’s speed as it passed through its lowest point. Each height was tested five times, and the class recorded the mean speed.

Before the experiment, the class used the law of conservation of energy to predict the speed at the lowest point if no energy were changed into other forms. The predicted and measured speeds are shown below.

Release height (m)Predicted speed, no friction (m/s)Measured mean speed (m/s)
0.202.01.9
0.402.82.7
0.804.03.8
1.605.65.4

Gravitational potential energy: PE = mgh, where g = 9.8 m/s2. Kinetic energy: KE = ½mv2.

She recorded the water temperature every 10 minutes for 30 minutes.

stimuli.title: Current Through Different Resistors
stimuli.html:
A student built a simple circuit with one battery, a switch, a current meter, and one resistor. She kept the same battery and wires for every trial and changed only the resistor. For each resistor, she closed the switch and recorded the current.

Resistance (Ω)Current (A)
3.03.0
6.01.5
9.01.0
180.50

Ohm’s law: V = IR, where V is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes (A), and R is resistance in ohms (Ω).

items.prompt: A battery-powered flashlight is switched on and shines a beam of light. Which sequence best describes the main energy conversions in the flashlight?
options: Chemical energy → electrical energy → light energy
Light energy → electrical energy → chemical energy
Electrical energy → chemical energy → nuclear energy
Thermal energy → chemical energy → light energy
items.hint: Start with where the energy is stored before the flashlight is turned on.
items.explain:
The battery stores chemical energy. When the switch closes, chemical reactions in the battery push charges through the circuit as electrical energy. The bulb changes the electrical energy into light energy (plus some thermal energy).

The reversed sequence (light → electrical → chemical) describes something like a solar charger filling a battery, not a flashlight in use. Nothing in a flashlight involves nuclear energy, and thermal energy is a by-product, not the starting form.

items.prompt: A cook leaves a metal spoon resting in a pot of simmering soup. A few minutes later, the end of the handle sticking out of the pot feels hot. By which process did thermal energy travel up the handle?
items.hint: The energy moved through a solid object, from one end to the other.
items.explain:
Heat moved through the solid metal by conduction: particles at the hot end vibrate faster and bump into neighboring particles, passing energy along the spoon to the handle. Metals are good conductors, so this happens quickly.

Convection requires a moving liquid or gas, so it explains how the soup itself circulates, not how heat moves through a solid spoon. Radiation is energy carried by electromagnetic waves across a gap, and evaporation is a change of state, not a way heat travels through a spoon.

items.prompt: Sort each example into the method of heat transfer it shows.
choices: A pan handle gets hot while the pan sits on a burner
Warm air from a floor heater rises and spreads through a room
Sunlight warms the seats of a parked car
You feel the heat of a campfire from several feet away
An ice pack held against your skin makes your skin cooler
Warm water in an ocean current flows north and warms the coast
items.hint: Touching = conduction. Moving liquid or gas = convection. Waves across a distance = radiation.
items.explain:
• Conduction (direct contact): the pan handle heating up; the ice pack against your skin (heat flows from your warmer skin into the cooler ice pack).
  • Convection (moving fluid): warm air rising and circulating from the heater; the moving ocean current carrying warm water.
  • Radiation (electromagnetic waves): sunlight warming the car seats; feeling a campfire’s heat from a distance. No touching and no moving fluid is needed.

A common mistake is to call the ice pack “cold flowing into the skin.” Heat always flows from warmer to cooler, so your skin loses heat to the ice pack by conduction.

items.prompt: A 60 kg runner is moving at a speed of 5.0 m/s. Kinetic energy can be calculated with the formula KE = ½mv2. What is the runner’s kinetic energy?
items.hint: Square the speed before you do anything else.
items.explain:
KE = ½mv2
v2 = 5.0 × 5.0 = 25
60 × 25 = 1,500
½ × 1,500 = 750 J

1,500 J comes from forgetting the ½. 150 J comes from not squaring the speed (½ × 60 × 5). 300 J is just mass × speed, which is not a kinetic energy formula.

items.prompt: Using PE = mgh, calculate the gravitational potential energy of the 0.50 kg pendulum ball when it is held at a release height of 0.80 m. Enter your answer in joules.
items.hint: Multiply the mass, 9.8, and the height.
items.explain:
PE = mgh
PE = 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.80
0.50 × 9.8 = 4.9
4.9 × 0.80 = 3.92 J

A common error is to leave out g and multiply only 0.50 × 0.80 = 0.40. The 9.8 m/s2 for gravity must be included.

items.prompt: At every release height, the measured speed was slightly lower than the predicted speed. Which statement best explains this result?
options: Some of the ball’s energy was changed into thermal energy by air resistance and friction at the point where the string was attached.
Some of the ball’s energy was destroyed as it swung toward its lowest point.
The ball’s mass increased as it swung downward, which slowed it down.
The ball gained extra potential energy as it moved toward its lowest point.
items.hint: Energy cannot disappear. Ask what other form some of it could have changed into.
items.explain:
The prediction assumed that all of the potential energy would become kinetic energy. In a real pendulum, air pushes against the moving ball and the string rubs where it is attached. These forces change a small amount of the energy into thermal energy (and a little sound), so less kinetic energy is left and the ball moves slightly slower.

“Energy was destroyed” is wrong because the law of conservation of energy says energy cannot be destroyed, only changed in form. The ball’s mass does not change, and the ball loses potential energy as it moves down; it does not gain any.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the cup-wrapping experiment.

The water in every mug cooled because thermal energy flowed from {{0}}. Over the 30 minutes, the mug wrapped in {{1}} lost the least thermal energy, so that material was the best {{2}} in the test.

options: the warmer water to the cooler room air
the cooler room air to the warmer water
the wrapping material into the water

items.hint: Heat always flows from warmer to cooler. Find the mug whose temperature dropped the fewest degrees.
items.explain:
The water started at 80 °C and the room was 22 °C, so heat flowed from the warmer water to the cooler room air. Heat never flows from cooler to warmer on its own.

Temperature drops over 30 minutes: no wrap 80 − 48 = 32 °C; foil 80 − 56 = 24 °C; wool 80 − 67 = 13 °C; foam 80 − 71 = 9 °C. The foam sleeve mug cooled the least, so foam slowed heat transfer the most. A material that slows heat transfer is an insulator; a conductor would speed it up.

items.prompt: A sound wave traveling through air has a frequency of 250 Hz and a wavelength of 1.36 m. Wave speed can be found with v = f × λ. What is the speed of the sound wave?
items.hint: Multiply the frequency by the wavelength.
items.explain:
v = f × λ
v = 250 × 1.36
250 × 1 = 250 and 250 × 0.36 = 90
250 + 90 = 340 m/s

183.8 m/s comes from dividing 250 by 1.36, and 0.0054 m/s comes from dividing 1.36 by 250. 251.36 m/s comes from adding the two numbers. The formula calls for multiplying. (340 m/s is a typical speed of sound in air, which is a good check.)

items.prompt: Which list places these types of electromagnetic waves in order from lowest frequency to highest frequency?
options: Radio waves, microwaves, visible light, X-rays
X-rays, visible light, microwaves, radio waves
Visible light, radio waves, X-rays, microwaves
Microwaves, radio waves, X-rays, visible light
items.hint: Radio waves have the longest wavelength. Longest wavelength means lowest frequency.
items.explain:
The electromagnetic spectrum, from longest wavelength (lowest frequency) to shortest wavelength (highest frequency), is: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. So the correct order is radio waves, microwaves, visible light, X-rays.

The choice beginning with X-rays lists the waves from highest to lowest frequency; it is exactly backward. The other two choices mix up the order.

items.prompt: The student uses the same battery with a new 12 Ω resistor. Based on the data and Ohm’s law, what current, in amperes, should she measure?
items.hint: First use any row of the table to find the battery’s voltage with V = IR.
items.explain:
Step 1: Find the battery voltage. Use any row, for example 3.0 A and 3.0 Ω:
V = I × R = 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0 V
(Check: 1.5 × 6.0 = 9.0, 1.0 × 9.0 = 9.0, 0.50 × 18 = 9.0.)

Step 2: Find the new current.
I = V ÷ R = 9.0 ÷ 12 = 0.75 A

A common error is to skip Step 1 or to assume current goes up with resistance. Ohm’s law shows that at the same voltage, more resistance gives less current.

items.prompt: Which conclusions are supported by the data? Select two answers.
options: Doubling the resistance from 9.0 Ω to 18 Ω cut the current in half.
For every trial, current × resistance equals 9.0, so the battery supplied about 9.0 V.
Current is directly proportional to resistance.
Increasing the resistance increased the current.
A 36 Ω resistor with the same battery would carry a current of 0.50 A.
items.hint: Multiply the current by the resistance in each row. What do you notice?
items.explain:
Supported:

  • At 9.0 Ω the current was 1.0 A; at 18 Ω it was 0.50 A. Doubling the resistance halved the current.
  • 3.0 × 3.0 = 9.0; 1.5 × 6.0 = 9.0; 1.0 × 9.0 = 9.0; 0.50 × 18 = 9.0. Since V = IR, the battery voltage was 9.0 V each time.

Not supported: Current went down as resistance went up, so it is not directly proportional and it did not increase. A 36 Ω resistor would carry I = 9.0 ÷ 36 = 0.25 A, not 0.50 A.

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg ball is dropped from rest from a height of 20 m. Ignore air resistance. Use PE = mgh (g = 9.8 m/s2) and KE = ½mv2. Assuming all of the ball’s potential energy changes into kinetic energy, what is its speed just before it hits the ground?
items.hint: Find the PE at the top first. Set that equal to KE, then solve for v. Do not forget the square root.
items.explain:
Step 1: PE at the top. PE = 2.0 × 9.8 × 20 = 392 J.

Step 2: Set KE equal to PE. 392 = ½ × 2.0 × v2
½ × 2.0 = 1.0, so 392 = 1.0 × v2
v2 = 392

Step 3: Take the square root. v = √392 ≈ 19.8 m/s

392 m/s comes from forgetting the square root. 14.0 m/s and 196 m/s come from leaving out the ½ in the KE formula (v2 = 392 ÷ 2.0 = 196, so v = 14.0, or 196 if the square root is also skipped).
